# AGENT.md — conventions for this repository

Read this before writing any code here. It is the contract that keeps generated applications consistent, and it is the reason a human can review an agent's PR quickly.

The stack is fixed: **C# on .NET 10, ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, EF Core with Npgsql, xUnit v3, and Blazor components rendered statically on the server for the screens.** Use .NET 10 APIs and idioms. If you remember an older way of doing something (Startup.cs, Swashbuckle, `IActionResult` controllers, Newtonsoft.Json), it is wrong here.

## Do not edit these

| Path | Why |
|---|---|
| `Dockerfile` | Defines the image contract the Terraform module depends on: port, non-root user, `/health`, the `migrate` argument. |
| `.github/workflows/` | CI is a guardrail on your output. You must not be able to weaken it. |
| `scripts/check-migrations.sh` | Same: it is the check on your migrations. |
| `scripts/check-test-layout.py`, `scripts/check-pages.py`, `.csharpierignore` | The checks behind "Conventions" and "Screens" below. |
| `src/App/Components/AppApi.cs`, `AppShell.razor`, `Routes.razor` | How pages reach data, and the document they render into. See "Screens". |
| `changes/`, `scripts/check-changes.sh`, `tests/App.Tests/Acceptance/` | The change record and its check. See "The change record" below. |
| `requests/` | Pending requests, written by the people who ask for changes. The harness moves one into `changes/` when its change starts. |
| `Directory.Build.props`, `global.json`, `.editorconfig` | Compiler and style settings. Warnings are errors on purpose. |
| `.aaas/deployment` | Set once when the repo is created. Changing it retargets deployments silently. |
| `preview.yml`, `scripts/preview*.sh`, `.run/`, `src/App/Properties/launchSettings.json` | The operator's workbench: how a branch is previewed and run from Rider. See README "The workbench". |
| `AGENT.md` | This file. |

If one of these genuinely needs to change, say so and stop. A human decides.

## The change record

A change starts as a request: `requests/<name>.md`, written by the requester from `requests/TEMPLATE.md` and committed to the default branch. Starting the change moves it into the record.

`changes/<id>/` holds one change to this application each: `brief.md`, the request it was built from, and acceptance tests written from that request by a spec-tester who never sees the code. The agent harness writes them, on the change's branch, before and after you work. You do not.

- **Read them.** The briefs are the history of what was asked for and why; the tests are the behaviour each change was accepted on. Your change must keep every earlier change's tests green.
- **Never edit them**, not even the current change's. If one of this change's acceptance tests fails, your code does not do what the request says: fix the code. If you are certain a test contradicts the request, quote the request, name the test and stop. If the request asks for behaviour an *earlier* change's test forbids, stop and say so: superseding accepted behaviour is a human decision.
- CI checks this (`scripts/check-changes.sh`): a merged record never changes, only commits carrying the harness's `AaaS-Change` trailer may touch `changes/`, and a change record without acceptance tests is red.

The acceptance tests compile into `tests/App.Tests` (it includes `changes/**/*.cs`) and run with the endpoint tests. They derive from `tests/App.Tests/Acceptance/AcceptanceBase.cs`, and they are black-box: HTTP in, JSON out.

## The health contract

`GET /health` must return 200 **without touching the database**, and it must do so within a few seconds of process start.

This is not a stylistic preference. The container's liveness and readiness probes hit this endpoint. If `/health` depends on Postgres, a database problem presents as a failed deployment and a rolled-back revision, and you will spend a long time debugging the wrong layer. Database connectivity belongs on `/ready`, which nothing depends on.

The one place allowed to require the database at startup is the `migrate` step below, which runs in a separate init container before the app starts.

## Structure

```
src/App/
  Program.cs              # composition and routes; entry point
  Components/
    AppApi.cs             # how pages call routes - do not change
    Layout/MainLayout.razor
    Pages/<Name>.razor    # one file per screen
  Data/
    AppDbContext.cs       # the data model
    Database.cs           # connection and Entra auth - do not change
    <Entity>.cs           # one file per entity
  Migrations/             # generated by dotnet ef - never hand-edit
tests/App.Tests/
  *Tests.cs
  Pages/<Name>PageTests.cs
```

Beyond a handful of routes, move them into `src/App/Endpoints/<Area>Endpoints.cs` as `MapXxxEndpoints(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)` extension methods, called from `Program.cs`. Do not introduce controllers.

## Schema changes — migrations

The data model changes only through EF Core migrations. The platform applies them before each new version starts; you never apply them yourself and never write DDL anywhere else.

To change the schema:

```bash
# 1. change the entity classes and/or AppDbContext
# 2. generate the migration - never write one by hand
#    (needs `dotnet restore` and `dotnet tool restore` to have run first)
dotnet ef migrations add <PascalCaseDescription> --project src/App
# 3. read the generated Up() method; it is what will run against live data
```

Rules, each enforced by CI:

- **Every model change has a migration.** `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` fails the build otherwise.
- **An applied migration is never edited, renamed or deleted.** It has run against a customer's database; if it was wrong, add a new migration that corrects it. A migration that is merged but has *not* been applied - typically one whose deploy failed and rolled back - may be corrected in place. CI knows which is which from the estate's applied record and says so. `AppDbContextModelSnapshot.cs` is the only file in `Migrations/` that changes, and only via `dotnet ef`.
- **Migrations are expand-only.** Add tables, add columns, add indexes. Do not drop or rename a table or column. Rollback means redeploying the previous image against the *current* schema, so the previous version of the code must still work after your migration. A new column must be nullable or have a default for the same reason.

If a request genuinely needs something removed or renamed, stop and say so. That is a two-release change (stop using it, then remove it later) and a human decides when the second half happens.

Seed or reference data goes in a migration too (`migrationBuilder.InsertData`), never in startup code.

Use snake_case table and column names, set explicitly in `OnModelCreating` as `AppDbContext` does for `items`.

## Rules

**Configuration comes from environment variables.** Read them through `IConfiguration`. `PGHOST`, `PGDATABASE`, `PGUSER`, `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` and `PORT` are injected by the platform; do not redefine them.

**There is no database password.** The container's managed identity requests a short-lived Entra token for each new connection. `Data/Database.cs` handles this — inject `AppDbContext` and do not write your own connection logic.

This is not merely a nicety. Any stored credential ends up in Terraform state and must be readable by whatever identity runs `terraform plan`, which broke the deployment pipeline twice before the credential was removed altogether. **Do not introduce a connection string, a Key Vault secret, or a Container App secret** — it fails at plan time, not at runtime, and the error will not mention this file.

**Database access is lazy.** Nothing may touch the database at startup: no `EnsureCreated`, no `Migrate`, no warm-up queries in `Program.cs`. See the health contract.

**Locally**, set `PGHOST=localhost` and `PGPASSWORD=...` to use ordinary password auth against a local Postgres. `PGPASSWORD` is for development only and is never set in the deployed environment.

**Pin every dependency.** Versions live only in `Directory.Packages.props`; `PackageReference` elements carry no `Version`. `packages.lock.json` is committed and CI restores in locked mode, so after adding or changing a package run `dotnet restore` and commit the updated lock files.

**Fail with a status code, not a stack trace.** Unreachable database is a 503 — `DatabaseUnavailableHandler` does this for you. Bad input is a 400: put `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations` attributes on the request record and validation runs before your handler does. Not found is a 404 (`Results.NotFound()`). An unhandled exception in a route is a bug.

**Request and response types are separate from entities.** Accept a `record` such as `ItemIn`; never bind a request body straight to an EF entity, or a client can set fields it should not.

**Every new or changed route gets an endpoint test against Postgres.** A test that only proves a route fails without a database, or that builds its own `IQueryable` and checks it, proves nothing about the route: three agent-written features passed exactly such tests with a bug in them. An endpoint test derives from `EndpointTest`, seeds rows, calls the route through `Client`, and asserts **exactly which rows come back, in order** — including at least one seeded row that must *not* come back. Each test gets its own empty, fully migrated database, so seed everything the test needs and assert the whole result, not "contains".

```csharp
public sealed class ItemSearchTests(TemplateDatabase template) : EndpointTest(template)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Search_matches_title_or_note_newest_first()
    {
        // Arrange
        await SeedAsync(
            new Item { Title = "Invoice March" }, // match on title
            new Item { Title = "Call", Note = "invoice" }, // match on note
            new Item { Title = "Groceries" } // must not come back
        );

        // Act
        var items = await Client.GetFromJsonAsync<List<Item>>("/items/search?q=invoice", Ct);

        // Assert
        Assert.Equal(["Call", "Invoice March"], items!.Select(i => i.Title));
    }
}
```

Assert on the response body the client receives (titles, ids, status codes), not on what is in the database afterwards, unless the route's whole job is to write.

Tests that need no database — validation (400s), pure logic, the health contract in `HealthTests.cs` — stay plain xUnit classes and do not derive from `EndpointTest`. Do not use the EF in-memory provider or SQLite to fake a database; CI rejects them, and they hide exactly the differences that break against Postgres.

Endpoint tests read `TEST_POSTGRES`. Where it is unset — including your own environment — they are **skipped, not passed**: you cannot run them, so write them carefully and let CI run them. Do not change the fixture in `tests/App.Tests/Postgres/`, and do not try to start a Postgres yourself. CI runs them against a real Postgres and fails if any is skipped or if none ran at all.

## Screens

The people who ask for changes use the application through its screens; they never see a route. **A change the user will use - something they will look at, add, edit or mark - gets its screen in the same pull request as its route.** A change with no use to a person on its own (a count another screen will show later) does not need one.

Screens are **Blazor components rendered statically on the server**: a request comes in, the page renders to HTML, the browser shows it; a form posts back to its page and the page redirects. There is no render mode, no `blazor.web.js`, no JavaScript, no Node toolchain. An interactive circuit (`InteractiveServer`) does not survive the platform scaling the app to zero, and WebAssembly is a second build.

**A page reaches data only through the routes.** Inject `AppApi` and call the route, exactly as a client would: `Api.GetAsync<List<Item>>("/items")`, `Api.PutAsync($"/items/{id}", new { title, note })`. Never inject `AppDbContext` in a component. The routes carry the rules (trimming, limits, what may be cleared), and the route's tests and the change's acceptance tests prove them; a page that wrote to the database itself would carry an untested copy of those rules. If a screen needs data no route returns, add the route, with its endpoint test, and call it.

`AppApi` throws if a page calls a path or method no route serves, so a wrong path fails the page's test instead of showing an empty list. A route's refusal (`400`) comes back as an `ApiResult` whose `Messages` are the route's own reasons; show them with `<Errors Result="..." />` and do not invent your own.

Rules, each checked by `scripts/check-pages.py`:

- **Paths.** `@page "/"` is the start page. Every other page path starts with `/app/` (`/app/items/{id:int}`), so a page never shares a path with a route.
- **No database, no interactivity.** Nothing under `Components/` names `AppDbContext`, `DbSet` or EF Core; nothing uses `@rendermode`, an interactive render mode or `<script>`.
- **Every page has a page test.** A class deriving from `PageTest` (in `tests/App.Tests/Pages/`) that calls `GetPageAsync<TheComponent>(path)` against seeded rows and asserts what the user sees. A page with a form also submits it with `SubmitFormAsync<TheComponent>(path, formName, ("Input.Title", "..."))`, once accepted and once refused. Page tests run with the endpoint tests, against Postgres.

```csharp
public sealed class HomePageTests(TemplateDatabase template) : PageTest(template)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Adding_an_item_shows_it_in_the_list()
    {
        // Act
        var html = await SubmitFormAsync<Home>("/", "new-item", ("Input.Title", "Buy paint"));

        // Assert
        Assert.Contains("Buy paint", html);
    }
}
```

Forms: `<EditForm Model="Input" FormName="..." OnSubmit="..." method="post">` with a `[SupplyParameterFromForm] private XxxForm Input { get; set; } = null!;` set to `new()` in `OnInitializedAsync` when null. Form classes are page-local and hold strings as typed; the route decides what is valid. A field left empty is sent as `null`, not `""`: a browser submits an empty field as an empty string, and the route stores what it is given (an empty note stored as `""` once showed as a blank cell where the request said "—"). Page tests submit an empty optional field at least once. After a successful submit, `Navigation.NavigateTo(...)` to the page the user should land on.

Keep screens plain: a heading, a list or a form inside `<div class="card">`, labels on every field, words a non-technical person uses ("Add item", not "POST"). The styles are in `AppShell.razor`; use its classes rather than adding your own.

**Say what each screen is.** Give every page a `<PageTitle>` a person understands ("Edit item"). The harness finds your screens from the pages your pull request adds or changes, checks them on the live app, and tells the user where to look by those titles. It says nothing about a change that has no screen.

## Conventions

House rules for code in this repository. Each one has a check in CI, so a rule here is never only a request.

**Formatting is CSharpier's.** Run `dotnet csharpier format .` before you commit; CI runs `dotnet csharpier check .` and fails on any difference. Do not hand-format around it, and do not use `dotnet format` for whitespace. Migrations and `changes/` are excluded (`.csharpierignore`): the first are generated, the second are frozen records.

**Tests: Arrange, Act, Assert.** Every test (`[Fact]` or `[Theory]`) has a block body laid out in three parts, each starting with its comment:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task Done_items_are_not_listed()
{
    // Arrange
    await SeedAsync(new Item { Title = "keep" }, new Item { Title = "gone", IsDone = true });

    // Act
    var items = await Client.GetFromJsonAsync<List<Item>>("/items?open=true", Ct);

    // Assert
    Assert.Equal(["keep"], items!.Select(i => i.Title));
}
```

- `// Arrange` is left out only when there is nothing to arrange.
- When the call under test is itself the assertion (a helper that asserts the status code), use one `// Act & Assert`.
- A note may follow a colon: `// Assert: 503, not a stack trace`.
- No expression-bodied tests (`=> ...`): there is nowhere to put the comments.

`scripts/check-test-layout.py` checks every test file a pull request adds or changes.

## Before you open a PR

```bash
dotnet restore
dotnet tool restore
dotnet csharpier format .
python3 scripts/check-test-layout.py --files <the test files you changed>
python3 scripts/check-pages.py
dotnet build -c Release
dotnet test -c Release --no-build
dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes --project src/App --no-build --configuration Release
docker build -t app:local .
```

Note that `dotnet ef` spells the build configuration `--configuration`: its `-c` means `--context`.

All must pass (endpoint tests show as skipped without `TEST_POSTGRES`; that is expected). CI runs the same commands, runs the endpoint tests against a real Postgres, plus the migration checks, a container smoke test, and your migrations applied twice to a throwaway Postgres — so a failure locally is a failure in CI. If `dotnet csharpier check .` reports differences, run `dotnet csharpier format .` and commit the result.

## What happens after merge

Merging to `master` builds an image tagged with the commit SHA, pushes it to GHCR, and opens a PR against `aaas-deployments` bumping `container_image`. That second PR is what actually deploys: the new revision's init container runs `migrate`, and the app container starts only if it succeeds. You do not need to do anything to trigger it, and you must not edit the deployments repo by hand to work around it.
